title: Sick, Well, Fit
subtitle: How companies should use AI: train to be fit, not just well
thesis: I strongly believe that AI is even more powerful to those that actually understand the fundamentals of the area they are applying AI to. Orders of magnitude more than the person vibing their way into a discipline AI gives them access to.
thesis_note: his belief, and the frame for this chapter; not a measured result
summary: Clark Huang's view is that AI is far more powerful in the hands of people who understand the fundamentals of the area they apply it to than for someone vibing their way in, and this chapter gives that view a picture: Greg Glassman's line from sickness through wellness to fitness. Most companies aim for well, a normal reading; fit is a margin, and making AI part of how a company operates is hard enough to need one. The chapter carries CrossFit's models over to a company one by one (markers, the hopper, three engines, work capacity, mechanics then consistency then intensity, the pyramid, virtuosity, benchmarks, scaling, luck, open scoring) and ends with "Business Fitness in 100 Words" and a rule a person or an agent can follow.
preview: Clark Huang's belief, above, is the frame for this chapter; it is his view, not a measurement. Vibing gets a company to well. Fundamentals plus AI gets it to fit. The picture is borrowed from CrossFit: sickness, wellness and fitness are one line, wellness is the middle of it, and fitness is a margin for the day something goes wrong. AI is intensity, so the order is the gym's: mechanics first, then consistency, and only then intensity. Choose markers you can observe, practice the draw you dread, time the same work every quarter, and ask for proof instead of "done".
hook: Most companies strive for well; AI rewards the ones that train to be fit: fundamentals first, then consistency, and only then intensity.
rule: Well is a reading and fit is a margin, so train for fit. Choose markers you can observe, time the same work every quarter, and practice the event you dread. Put AI on fundamentals you understand: mechanics first, then consistency, and only then intensity. In full: when you report how a team, a system, or an agent’s work is doing, do not start with a feeling. Name the markers, give each a reading of sick, well, or fit, and show evidence someone else can check. If one marker is moving the wrong way while the others improve, say that first, and investigate it first. Before you start a plan, write down the measurement you expect, and afterward say whether it came true. Keep a short list of benchmark work, hold the work the same, time it every quarter, and post the times. Name the event you least want to draw, and rehearse it. Turn AI, scope, or speed up only where three things hold: someone understands the fundamentals well enough to tell when the output is wrong; the mechanics are right; and the result passes the same check without a hero. Scale the load to the size of the team and keep the movement. Plan the slack. Fitness improves the odds. It does not remove bad luck.
frame: Nonfiction, from the how-to half of the book: Clark Huang's views, with sources. CrossFit's models are borrowed as a lens. Not affiliated with or endorsed by CrossFit; CrossFit is a trademark of CrossFit, LLC. The made-up company is an illustration.
video_blurb: The whole chapter as a videobook: every gym idea shown next to its business match, from a blood-pressure gauge beside a company dashboard to a botched lift beside an AI rollout breaking. It ends on Business Fitness in 100 Words.
